title: Fatherhood — Holding, Carrying, Teaching
hook: A child learns what a man's body means long before he learns words: from how he is held, carried, met at eye level and taught with hands.
why:
For a baby, a father is first of all a body: a chest, a pair of arms, a voice felt through a ribcage, a heartbeat, a smell. For a toddler, he is a height to be lifted to and a hand to be held. For a child, he is a pair of hands showing how a thing is done, and a body that either comes down to meet him or stays up out of reach. Long before any conversation about feelings or values, a child has learned from his father's body whether he is safe, whether he is welcome, and what men do with their hands.

This chapter is about fatherhood as a physical skill. It covers how men's bodies change when they become fathers; holding a baby, and why skin and a steady chest matter; what to do when the crying will not stop, including the one rule that must never be broken; coming down to a child's level and the cost of a still, unresponsive face; rough-and-tumble play and what it teaches; teaching with hands without taking over; and the child's right to their own body. Much of it applies to any man who cares for children: uncles, stepfathers, grandfathers, coaches and teachers.

teach.p:
It is often assumed that the biology of parenthood belongs to mothers. Research on fathers suggests that men's bodies respond as well. In a study published in 2011, Lee Gettler, Christopher Kuzawa and their colleagues followed several hundred young men in Cebu, in the Philippines, for about four and a half years. The men who became fathers during that time showed the steepest falls in testosterone, and earlier work in the same group had linked lower testosterone in fathers with more involvement in childcare.

The researchers suggested that the fall may help shift men's priorities from competing for mates toward caring for children. The study was observational, and testosterone is only one part of a complicated picture. But it challenges the idea that men are biologically sidelined in parenting. Fathers' bodies, like mothers', seem to adjust to the work.

The rest of this chapter is about that work, which is largely physical. Holding a baby, carrying a toddler on one hip while doing something with the other hand, walking at a child's pace, kneeling to tie a shoe, catching a child who jumps off a wall: fatherhood is done with the body, and children read every movement of it.

The figure here stands with a young child on his hip, the hip pushed out to take the weight, one arm wrapped under the child. It is one of the commonest postures of fathering, and from across a room it is often the first thing that marks a man as a father.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's hormones showed no change on becoming fathers. Gettler and colleagues found a marked change, though in one population, and what it means for behaviour is still debated.

teach.p:
In a small trial published in 2007, Kerstin Erlandsson and her colleagues in Sweden studied healthy babies born by planned caesarean section, whose mothers could not hold them straight away. The babies were placed either skin to skin on their father's chest or in a cot beside him. The babies held skin to skin cried much less, and calmed down and became drowsy sooner.

The study was small, but it fits what many fathers discover: a baby held against a bare chest, hearing a heartbeat and feeling warmth and steady breathing, often settles when nothing else works. The chapter on breath in Part II described how one person's breathing can steady another's. A father's slow breath, felt through his chest, is one of the first ways a baby borrows calm.

Holding a young baby has one firm rule: support the head and neck, because for the first few months a baby cannot hold its own head up. Hold the baby close against your body, upright against your chest with a hand behind the head, or cradled in the crook of an arm.

Holding is also the start of conversation. Researchers at Harvard's Center on the Developing Child describe the back-and-forth between a baby and a caregiver, a babble answered by a voice, a look answered by a smile, as serve and return, and argue that it shapes the developing brain. The figure here holds a baby against his chest, head bowed toward it. Every sound the baby makes is a serve. A father's job is to return it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if babies held skin to skin by their fathers settled no better than babies placed in a cot. Erlandsson and colleagues found that they did, but in a trial of only 29 babies, so the result is encouraging rather than conclusive.

teach.h: When the crying will not stop.
teach.p:
All babies cry, and many cry a great deal. Crying typically increases from about two weeks of age, peaks around the second month, and eases by three to five months. Some babies cry for hours, especially in the evening, and nothing seems to help. The programme known as the Period of PURPLE Crying was developed to help parents understand that this is normal.

It is also exhausting, and exhaustion and frustration can build into something dangerous. Shaking a baby, even briefly, can cause brain damage or death. The UK programme known as ICON gives four simple messages: infant crying is normal; comforting methods can help; it is okay to walk away; never, ever shake a baby.

Walking away is the skill. If you feel anger or desperation rising, put the baby down safely on its back in a cot, leave the room, and calm yourself for a few minutes: breathe slowly, splash your face, put on music, call someone. Then go back and check on the baby. A crying baby in a safe cot is not in danger. A baby held by an adult who has lost control is.

The earlier chapters on silence and disagreement described flooding, the state of overwhelm in which thinking breaks down. A father at three in the morning with a screaming baby is a prime candidate. Learn your own signs, and step away before they peak. If the crying worries you, or you are not coping, speak to your doctor, midwife or health visitor, or a health line where you live. The figure here covers his eyes, exhausted. Every father reaches this point; what matters is what he does next.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if putting a crying baby down and stepping away were unsafe or harmful. Health services widely recommend it as a way to prevent shaking injuries, though no single study can show how many injuries it prevents.
teach.pullQuote: A crying baby in a safe cot is not in danger. A baby held by an adult who has lost control is.

teach.p:
A man standing over a small child is a giant. His face is a long way up, his voice comes from above, and his hands can reach down and lift the child whether the child wants it or not. Children read this height, and many of the simplest improvements in a father's communication come from removing it. Kneel, squat or sit so that your eyes are at the child's level, especially when they are upset, when you are setting a limit, or when you are listening to something that matters to them.

What your face does at that level matters as much as the height. In the 1970s Edward Tronick and his colleagues asked mothers to face their babies and then suddenly hold their faces still and unresponsive. Within seconds the babies tried harder to engage, then grew distressed and turned away. The procedure, known as the still face, has since been used in many studies, including with fathers. A baby needs a face that answers.

Older children need the same. A father who listens with a still face, or with his eyes on a phone, is offering a milder version of the still face, and children notice. Put the phone down, come down to their height, and let your face respond to what they are telling you.

The figures here show an adult down on one knee facing a small child, their heads level. It is one of the simplest things a father can do with his body, and one of the most powerful.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if babies showed no distress when a caregiver's face stopped responding. The still-face studies consistently find that they do; whether everyday phone use has similar effects is a reasonable inference rather than an established finding.

teach.p:
Many fathers play physically: chasing, tickling, wrestling on the floor, throwing a child in the air, piggyback rides. In 2020 Paulina Amodia-Bidakowska, Ciara Laverty and Paul Ramchandani reviewed 78 studies of father-child play carried out over four decades. They found that fathers tended to play more physically than mothers, even with very young children, and that father-child play was consistently associated with children's later ability to manage their feelings and behaviour.

The researchers were careful: the findings are correlational, so they cannot show that play causes better self-control, and mothers can play physically too. One idea is that rough play gives children an exciting, safe setting in which to practise keeping control: getting wound up and calming down, winning and losing, playing hard without hurting.

That only works if the adult keeps the play safe and fair. Research on rough-and-tumble play suggests that its benefits depend on the father being in charge of the game: setting limits, stopping when it gets too wild, not letting it tip into real aggression. And it depends on consent, as the chapter on consent described: when a child says stop, the play stops, every time, even when they are laughing.

The figure here opens his arms wide, ready to catch or to be charged at. Physical play is one of the great pleasures of fathering. Done well, it also teaches a child that strength can be gentle and that a man's power can be held in check.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if father-child play showed no association with children's self-regulation. The review found a consistent association, but in correlational studies, so play may reflect other good things in a relationship rather than cause them.

teach.p:
In 1976 David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross watched tutors helping young children build a tricky wooden puzzle, and described what good tutoring looked like. They called it scaffolding. The tutor recruited the child's interest, simplified the task, kept the child pointed toward the goal, marked the important features, controlled frustration and demonstrated when needed, and then gradually withdrew help as the child became able to do more.

Much of scaffolding is physical. Where you put your body decides whether a child keeps the task or loses it to you. Beside the child, at their height, with your hands near the job but not on it, the child stays in charge. Behind them, with your hands over theirs, you are doing it for them. Standing over them and pointing, you are a supervisor, not a teacher.

Watch for your own frustration as the child struggles. It shows in your breath, your jaw and your hands, and children read it instantly. When you feel the urge to grab the tool and do it yourself, sit on your hands for a moment. Let the child try again. Step in with the smallest help that will work, and step out again as soon as you can.

The figures here show an adult kneeling beside a child, both facing the same task, the adult's hand near the child's but not taking over. It is the posture of a teacher who wants the child, not himself, to succeed.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if children learned as well when an adult took over the task as when an adult supported them to do it. Research on scaffolding and learning suggests they do not, though how much help is right depends on the child and the task.

teach.p:
A child learns from the earliest age whether their body belongs to them. Every time an adult stops tickling when they say stop, lets them choose a high five instead of a kiss for a visiting aunt, asks before picking them up when they are old enough to answer, or knocks before entering their room as they grow, the child learns that their no works. Every time their no is overridden, they learn the opposite.

This matters for safety. Children who know that their body is theirs, and that they can tell a trusted adult when something feels wrong, are better placed to resist and report abuse. Child-protection organisations teach exactly this, often to children of nursery age.

It also matters for sons in particular. Many fathers hug and kiss their small sons freely and then stop, somewhere around the age of eight or ten, as if affection between a man and a boy must end. The chapters on the bro hug and on touch between friends described what that does to men. Keep offering a hug, an arm across the shoulders, a hand on the back, as your son grows, and let him choose the form. You are teaching him how men touch with consent.

The figures here walk hand in hand, the adult's hand lowered to the child's height. Walking at a child's pace, with a hand they can take or let go of, is a small daily lesson in what a man's body can be: strong, steady, and on the child's terms.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if children's early experience of having their no respected made no difference to how they protected themselves later. The principle is central to child-protection guidance, though rigorous long-term evidence on its effects is limited.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Head down to a phone while the baby babbles
poseGallery.annotation: A baby's babble is a serve. Put the phone down, hold the baby close and answer with your voice and face.

poseGallery.doCaption: Beside him, at his height, hands near
poseGallery.annotation: Where you put your body decides who owns the task. Beside and level, the child keeps it; above and pointing, you take it.
To a small child, a standing man is a giant. Kneel or squat, and let your face answer what he is telling you.

poseGallery.doCaption: Kneeling to her level, voice low
poseGallery.dontCaption: Arms folded over a screaming toddler
poseGallery.annotation: From above, a father is a giant telling her off. At her level, calm, he is someone she can come back to when the storm passes.

poseGallery.doCaption: Settled, breathing slowly, baby on his chest
poseGallery.dontCaption: Checking the clock while jiggling the baby
poseGallery.annotation: A baby borrows calm from the body holding her. A slow breath and a steady chest often settle her when nothing else will.

poseGallery.doCaption: Walking hand in hand at his pace
poseGallery.dontCaption: Carrying him everywhere, doing it for him
poseGallery.annotation: Letting a child do it himself, with you alongside, teaches more than doing it for him, however much quicker that would be.

caseStudy:
Kamal, thirty-three, becomes a father in October. By the sixth week, his daughter Leila cries for three or four hours every evening, and his wife is exhausted. Kamal takes the night shifts at weekends. One night at three in the morning, after two hours of walking and rocking, he feels something he has never felt before: a hot surge of anger at a tiny screaming person. It frightens him. He remembers the leaflet from the hospital. He lays Leila on her back in her cot, walks into the kitchen, runs cold water over his wrists and breathes until the anger drains. Five minutes later he goes back. She is still crying, and he is calm. He takes his shirt off and holds her against his chest, and after a while she sleeps.

He tells the health visitor about the anger, expecting to be judged. She tells him that what he did was exactly right.

Three years later Kamal is teaching Leila to ride a bike. His instinct is to grip the handlebars and run alongside steering. He makes himself let go of the bars and jog beside her with a hand hovering near her back, not touching. She wobbles, falls, cries, and gets back on. On the fourth day she rides to the end of the path on her own and turns round shrieking.

That evening, in a tickle fight on the sofa, Leila shouts, “Stop, Daddy, stop!” through her laughter. Kamal stops at once. She looks at him, thinks, and says, “Okay, again.” Kamal's own father never hugged him after he was about nine. He has decided that Leila will choose when the hugs stop, not him.
observe: Notice how adults around you position their bodies with small children: standing over, kneeling, side by side.
Notice the serve and return between a parent and a baby: the babble, the look, the answer, or the answer that does not come.
Notice your own frustration when a child struggles with a task, and what your hands want to do.
Notice how often a child's stop is respected during play, by you or others.

drills.name: Eye Level
steps: For one day, whenever you talk to a child about something that matters, come down to their eye level first.
Notice how the child's face and body respond.
Notice how your own voice changes when you are no longer talking down.
Write down one difference you noticed.
variations: Do the eye-level drill when giving a child good news, not only when they are upset, and notice their face.
Notice how other adults speak to children in a park or a shop, and how often they come down to the child's level.

drills.name: Walk Away Plan
steps: Write down the signs in your own body that you are reaching the end of your patience: breath, jaw, heat, voice.
Write down where you would put a crying baby safely, and where you would go for a few minutes.
Write down three things that calm you quickly.
Save the number of a health line, doctor or health visitor in your phone.
If you share care with a partner, agree on a signal that means take over now.
variations: Write down who you would ring at three in the morning if you needed help, and save their number.
Share your walk-away plan with your partner, so that either of you can use it without explaining.

drills.name: Hands Off
steps: Choose a task a child is learning: tying laces, riding a bike, cooking, a puzzle.
Position yourself beside the child, at their height, hands near but not on the task.
Each time you want to take over, wait ten seconds and offer the smallest help that would work instead.
Withdraw help as soon as the child manages a step.
Afterwards, note how much of the task the child did themselves.
variations: Try the hands-off drill with a task you are very good at, which makes taking over even more tempting.
Ask your child afterwards what they liked about doing the task, and listen without correcting them.

drills.name: Their Choice
steps: Next time you greet a child you know, offer a choice: a hug, a high five or a wave.
Accept whatever they choose without comment.
In play, stop the moment they say stop, and wait for them to restart it.
Notice how the child responds over several weeks.
variations: Let your child choose how to greet a visiting relative for a month, and notice what they choose.
Agree a family rule that stop means stop in every game, and stick to it yourself.

quiz.q: Someone says that only a mother can really calm a newborn, because fathers lack the biology for it. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; studies show fathers have no calming effect on newborns
Babies held skin to skin by fathers cried less than babies in a cot
Fathers calm newborns better than mothers, because they hold them more firmly
Newborns cannot tell the difference between being held and lying in a cot
quiz.explain: In Erlandsson's trial, caesarean-born babies held skin to skin on their fathers' chests cried less and calmed sooner than those placed in a cot. Gettler's research also suggests that fathers' bodies adjust to caregiving.

quiz.q: What did Gettler and colleagues find when they followed young men in Cebu over several years?
options: Testosterone rose sharply in men who became fathers during the study
Becoming a father had no measurable effect on men's hormones at all
Men who became fathers showed the steepest falls in testosterone
Only men who were already low in testosterone went on to become fathers
quiz.explain: The men who became fathers showed the largest declines in testosterone, and earlier work linked lower testosterone in fathers with more involvement in childcare. Fathers' bodies seem to adjust to the work of caring.

quiz.q: At three in the morning your baby has cried for two hours and you feel anger rising. What should you do?
options: Hold the baby more tightly and keep rocking until the crying finally stops
Give the baby a firm, short shake, so that the crying stops before you lose it
Leave the house for an hour, so that you can come back properly calm
Put the baby down safely in the cot, step away a few minutes, then go back
quiz.explain: Putting a crying baby down safely and stepping away for a few minutes is the recommended response when frustration rises. Never shake a baby, even briefly; it can cause brain damage or death.

quiz.q: What happened in Tronick's still-face studies when a parent's face went still and unresponsive?
options: The babies tried to engage, then became distressed and turned away
The babies took no notice and carried on exactly as before
The babies became calmer, because the parent's face was less busy
The babies immediately fell asleep, since nothing was happening
quiz.explain: Babies tried harder to engage, then grew distressed and withdrew. A baby needs a face that answers, and older children notice a parent whose face, or whose eyes, are somewhere else.

quiz.q: What did the 2020 review of father-child play by Amodia-Bidakowska and colleagues find?
options: Physical play with fathers was linked with more aggression in children later on
Father-child play was consistently linked with children's later self-regulation
Fathers rarely played physically with children under the age of five
Play with fathers made no difference once mothers' play was taken into account
quiz.explain: Across 78 studies, fathers played more physically, and father-child play was consistently associated with children's later ability to manage feelings and behaviour. The findings are correlational, so they do not prove that play causes the benefit.

quiz.q: You are teaching your daughter to tie her laces and she keeps getting it wrong. You feel the urge to do it for her. What fits this chapter best?
options: Kneel behind her and tie them with your hands over hers each time
Stand over her and give clear instructions until she gets it right
Stay beside her, wait, and offer the smallest help that will work
Tie them yourself and teach her another day when she is older
quiz.explain: Scaffolding means doing just enough to keep a child moving, at their level and beside them, and withdrawing help as they manage more. Taking over teaches her that the task belongs to you.

quiz.q: What did Wood, Bruner and Ross call the kind of help good tutors gave young children?
options: Scaffolding, gradually withdrawn as the child can do more
Modelling, in which the tutor completes the whole task while the child watches
Correction, in which every mistake is pointed out and fixed by the adult at once
Free play, in which the tutor stays away and lets the child work entirely alone
quiz.explain: Wood, Bruner and Ross described scaffolding: recruiting interest, simplifying, demonstrating when needed and controlling frustration, then withdrawing help as the child becomes able to do more. The aim is for the child to keep the task.

quiz.q: Your three-year-old throws herself on the supermarket floor, screaming, because you said no to sweets. People are watching. What fits this chapter best?
options: Give her the sweets quickly so that the scene ends and everyone can move on
Pick her up at once and carry her out, telling her she is being naughty
Keep her safe, crouch to her level, stay calm and hold the limit until it passes
Stand over her and tell her firmly that people are looking at her
quiz.explain: Coming down to her level, keeping your own body calm and holding the limit without anger lets the storm pass and teaches her that tantrums do not change the answer. Safety comes first, then calm.

quiz.q: Someone says that because rough play is good for children, throwing a young baby high in the air is fine. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since babies need rough play as much as older children do
Rough play suits older children; babies need head support and must never be shaken
It is right, but only if the baby is laughing while it happens
It is wrong, since all physical play with children of any age is harmful
quiz.explain: The benefits of rough-and-tumble come with older children and an adult in charge. Young babies need their heads and necks supported, and must never be shaken.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific child in your life, your own or another you care for. Describe how you usually use your body with them: how you hold or greet them, your height when you talk, how you play, how you teach. Then think about your own father, or the man who was closest to being one. What did his body teach you about being held, being taught and having your no respected? Describe one physical habit you want to keep and one you want to change.
reflection.guidance: Be concrete about movements: kneeling or standing, hands on or hands near, stopping or carrying on. If your own father's body taught you fear, or nothing at all, that is worth writing about, and you are not bound to repeat it. If the reflection brings up painful memories, take care of yourself, and use the support resources in this app if you need them.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat a baby's crying as a test of will, and to keep holding on while anger builds, when the safe response is to put the baby down safely, step away and come back; and never, under any circumstances, to shake a baby. The second is to stay up at adult height, talking down to a child, or to listen with a still face or eyes on a phone. The third is to take over: teaching from behind with your hands on theirs, or from above with a pointing finger, so that the child loses the task. The fourth is to let rough play run without limits, or to carry on when a child says stop. And the fifth is to stop hugging a son as he grows, teaching him that affection between men ends in childhood.

moreCases.title: The father who handed her back
moreCases.scene:
Ollie, thirty, has a four-week-old daughter, Isla. Every time Isla cries, Ollie holds her for a minute or two, jiggling her a little stiffly, and then hands her back to his partner, Beth, saying that Isla wants her mum. Beth is exhausted, recovering from a difficult birth, and has started to resent it. She tells her sister that Ollie is happy to hold the baby when she is quiet but never when she needs settling.

Ollie, for his part, is frightened. When Isla cries in his arms, he feels clumsy and useless, and he is sure that he is doing something wrong. He has read that babies recognise their mother's smell and voice, and he has decided that there is no point in his trying.

One evening, Beth has a fever and has to go to bed early. Isla starts crying at eight o'clock, and there is nobody to hand her to.

Ollie's own father worked away for most of his childhood, and Ollie has no memory of being held by him. He has told Beth that he wants to be a different kind of father, and has no idea how.

Beth has also noticed that Ollie holds Isla away from his body when she cries, at arm's length, as if she were something that might break. When Isla is asleep, he holds her close and gazes at her for ages.
moreCases.misread:
Ollie read Isla's crying in his arms as proof that she needed her mother and that he could not help. Beth read his handing her back as unwillingness. Both readings assumed that soothing a baby was a gift some people had, rather than a skill that could be learned.

He also read his own fear as a lack of ability, when it was mostly a lack of practice. Every father is clumsy with a newborn at first.

And Beth's resentment, though fair, was also a reading through exhaustion. She saw unwillingness where there was mostly fear, and Ollie could not tell her, because he was ashamed of it.
moreCases.betterRead: Research on fathers suggests that men's bodies respond to parenthood too, and that fathers can comfort babies well. In Erlandsson's small Swedish trial, babies held skin to skin on their fathers' chests after a caesarean birth cried much less and calmed sooner than babies in a cot. Ollie's stiffness and quick handovers gave Isla little chance to settle against him, and gave him no chance to learn what worked. The better reading was that comforting a baby takes practice, time and a calm body, and that his fear was part of what Isla was feeling. That evening, with no one else, Ollie took off his shirt, held Isla against his bare chest with a hand behind her head, and walked slowly round the living room, breathing as slowly as he could. It took twenty minutes. Then she fell asleep on him. He did not move for an hour. After that, he took the evening settling three nights a week, and Beth said it was the first time since the birth she had felt they were in it together.

moreCases.title: The tickle that went on too long
moreCases.scene:
Rob, thirty-eight, loves rough play with his son Leo, six: wrestling on the sofa, chasing round the garden, tickle fights at bedtime. One Saturday morning, Rob pins Leo on the bed and tickles him. Leo shrieks with laughter and says, "Stop! Stop!" Rob keeps going, because Leo is laughing. Leo says stop again, louder, still laughing, and starts kicking. Rob laughs too and carries on for a few more seconds. Then Leo's laughter turns into crying, and he curls up and says that he hates his dad.

Rob is stunned and a little hurt. Leo was laughing. He thought they were having fun.

Rob's partner, Jo, who heard it from the kitchen, comes in and picks Leo up. Over his head, she gives Rob a look that he does not understand.

Rob was tickled relentlessly as a child by his older brothers, and remembers it as hilarious. He has never wondered whether he enjoyed it as much as he remembers.

Leo has been asking, for a few weeks, not to have tickle fights at bedtime. Jo heard him say it once and mentioned it to Rob, who laughed and said that Leo always ended up loving it. On Saturday morning, Leo had said "No tickling" before they started wrestling, and Rob had grinned and said, "We'll see."
moreCases.misread:
Rob read Leo's laughter as enjoyment and his "stop" as part of the game. He did not know that tickling causes laughter whether or not it is enjoyed, so Leo's laughing told him nothing about whether Leo wanted it to continue.

He also read his own childhood as proof that tickling was harmless, and did not ask whether Leo might feel differently from him.

And his "We'll see" when Leo had said no tickling before they started told Leo, before anything happened, that his no was open to negotiation.

Jo's look, which he did not understand, was the look of someone who had seen the same thing before and had been waiting for him to notice.
moreCases.betterRead:
The chapter on consent described this exactly: a child who is tickled will often laugh while saying stop, because tickling produces laughter regardless of whether it is wanted. The kicking and the louder stop were Leo's body backing up his words. Rough play has real value, and Amodia-Bidakowska and colleagues found father-child play associated with children's later self-control, but its benefit depends on the adult keeping it safe and fair, and on the child's no working. When Rob carried on, Leo learned that his no did not count when his father was enjoying himself. Rob's better response, once Jo explained, was to repair it and change the rule. He sat on the floor beside Leo, at his level, and said, "I'm sorry. I should have stopped when you said stop. From now on, stop means stop, straight away." The next time they played, Rob stopped the instant Leo said stop, and Leo, delighted with his new power, said stop about forty times, and started again each time.

Rob also told Jo that he had never thought about it before, and asked her to tell him if he got it wrong again.

moreCases.title: The science project
moreCases.scene:
Marcus, forty-two, is an engineer. His daughter, Amara, ten, has a school project: build a model of a working water wheel. They sit at the kitchen table on a Saturday afternoon with card, glue, a cork and some skewers. Amara starts cutting the paddles, slowly and unevenly. Marcus watches, his jaw tightening. After a few minutes, he says, "Here, let me show you," takes the scissors and cuts the rest of the paddles himself, neatly. Then he works out the axle, glues the wheel and tests it under the tap.

By the end of the afternoon, the water wheel works beautifully. Amara has spent most of it on her phone, sitting a little back from the table. When her mother asks how the project went, she shrugs and says, "Dad did it."

At school on Monday, her teacher praises the model. Amara does not mention that she barely touched it.

Amara had been excited about the project all week. She had drawn a design in her notebook, with paddles shaped like leaves, which she meant to show her father. She never got the chance.

Marcus also noticed, as he took the scissors, that Amara's shoulders dropped and she looked away. He thought it was relief. It was, he realised later, the moment she stopped being part of the project.
moreCases.misread:
Marcus read Amara's slow, uneven cutting as a problem to be solved, and his taking over as help. He did not notice that his body had moved from beside her to over the task, and that she had withdrawn as he did.

He also read the working model as success, when the point of the project was for Amara to learn how a water wheel works, which she had not.

And Amara's phone was not rudeness or laziness. It was what a ten-year-old does when she has been made a spectator at her own project.
moreCases.betterRead: Wood, Bruner and Ross described good teaching as scaffolding: recruiting the child's interest, simplifying the task, keeping them pointed at the goal, controlling frustration, demonstrating when needed and then withdrawing help as the child can do more. Much of it is physical. With his hands on the scissors and the glue, Marcus was doing the project, not teaching it, and Amara moved back from the table and onto her phone because there was nothing left for her to do. His tightening jaw was his own frustration, which children read instantly. The better approach was to keep the task in her hands. The next weekend, for a different project, Marcus sat beside Amara, at her height, with his hands on the table near the job but not on it. When she struggled, he asked, "What do you think the problem is?" and once, when she was stuck, showed her on a spare piece of card and gave it back. The result was wonky. Amara explained every part of it to her teacher, and asked if they could build another.

moreCases.title: The stepson who pulled away
moreCases.scene:
Gav, thirty-six, moved in with his partner, Sarah, and her son, Tyler, nine, six months ago. Gav is warm and physical by nature. He ruffles Tyler's hair, puts an arm round his shoulders, picks him up and swings him round, as he does with his own nephews. Tyler stiffens each time. He ducks away from the hair-ruffling, leans out from under the arm, and once, when Gav lifted him without warning, kicked out and shouted, "Put me down!"

Gav is hurt. He tells Sarah that Tyler does not like him and never will. Sarah says that Tyler is just shy, and that Gav should keep trying.

Gav tries harder: more hugs, more lifting, more arms round shoulders. Tyler starts spending more time in his room when Gav is home.

Tyler's own father left when he was four, and he sees him every other weekend. He has told his mum that he does not need a new dad. Sarah has not told Gav this.

Tyler has also started asking his mum whether Gav is staying "for ever", and whether his real dad knows that Gav lives with them now. He asked the question at bedtime, twice, with the light off, which Sarah has learned is when he says the things that worry him most.
moreCases.misread:
Gav read Tyler's stiffening and ducking as rejection of him, and Sarah read it as shyness to be overcome with persistence. Both readings led to more touch, when Tyler's body was asking for less.

And Sarah's advice to keep trying, given out of love for both of them, pushed Gav towards the response most likely to make Tyler withdraw.

Gav also read Tyler's withdrawal to his room as a sign that he was failing, which made him try harder, which made Tyler withdraw more: a loop in which each of them read the other's response as a reason to keep doing the thing that made it worse.
moreCases.betterRead:
A child learns from the earliest age whether their body belongs to them, and a new adult in the home, however kind, is someone whose touch the child has not yet chosen. Tyler's stiffness, his ducking and his shout of "Put me down!" were clear signals, the same signals the chapter on touch between friends described in adults: this is too much, too soon. Trying harder overrode them, and Tyler withdrew further. The better approach was to let Tyler set the pace. Gav stopped initiating touch altogether, apart from a high five if Tyler offered one. Instead, he offered things to do side by side: fixing Tyler's bike, playing football in the park, building a model together. He asked before any touch: "High five?" Over the next few months, Tyler started sitting next to him on the sofa during matches. One evening, after a goal, he leaned against Gav's arm and stayed there. Gav did not move or say anything about it.

Sarah also told Gav what Tyler had said about not needing a new dad, which helped him stop taking the distance personally.

workedReading.title: The meltdown in the supermarket
workedReading.scene:
Femi, thirty-five, is doing the weekly shop with his daughter, Ada, three. At the checkout, Ada asks for a packet of sweets. Femi says no. Ada throws herself on the floor, screaming, kicking her legs and arms, her face red and wet. The queue behind them goes quiet. A woman tuts. An older man says, loudly, that in his day children knew how to behave. Femi feels his face burn and his heart race. He wants, more than anything, to make it stop, by picking her up and leaving, or by giving her the sweets.

Femi has had a long week, and Ada has been unsettled since starting nursery. He knows that this tantrum is partly about the sweets and partly about everything else, and that he is running on empty too.

Ada has been at nursery since September and comes home tired and fractious most days. Femi suspects she has been holding herself together all week, and that the sweets were only the last straw.

He also knows that if he gives in today, the same scene will happen at the next checkout, and the one after that. The limit he holds now is a gift to himself next week.

steps.label: Check your own body first
steps.text:
Femi notices his own state: hot face, racing heart, tight jaw, the urge to grab. He knows from Part II that a stressed adult makes a stressed child worse, and that anything he does in the next few seconds will be done through embarrassment. He breathes out slowly, once, and lets his shoulders drop before he does anything else.

He also notices that the audience is affecting him more than Ada is. Her screaming is ordinary for a three-year-old; it is the tutting that makes his face burn.

He also reminds himself what the tutting woman and the older man do not know: that this is normal for a three-year-old, and that every parent in the queue has either been here or will be.

steps.label: Make her safe
steps.text:
He checks that Ada is not in danger: she is on the floor, away from the trolley wheels, not near anything she could hit. He moves the trolley slightly so that nobody will trip over her. Safety comes first, before anything about the limit or the audience.

He also keeps half an eye on the people around them, without engaging with them. He does not need to explain himself to the queue; he needs to keep his daughter safe.

He also checks that her head is not near the hard edge of the checkout counter. Children in a tantrum can throw their heads back suddenly, and moving her a few inches away is the most important thing he does.

steps.label: Come down to her level
steps.text:
He crouches down beside her, at her height, rather than standing over her. He does not grab her or try to lift her. From above, he would be a giant telling her off; at her level, he is her father, near her, with a face she can see.

He also crouches slightly to the side of her rather than directly over her, so that she has room to move and he is not blocking her.

He also keeps his hands visible and still, near her but not on her. Grabbing a child mid-tantrum often makes the storm worse, because it adds a fight to a feeling.

steps.label: Keep your face and voice calm
steps.text:
He keeps his face soft and his voice low and slow. He says, "You really wanted those sweets. You're cross." He does not argue, explain, threaten or bargain. Tronick's still-face studies showed how much small children need a face that answers, and Femi's answers: concerned, calm, not angry.

He also resists the urge to say "Stop it" or "Everyone's looking", which would add shame to her anger without helping her through it.

He also keeps his own breathing slow and audible, even though his heart is racing. Small children often borrow the rhythm of the adult nearest them, as the chapter on breath described.

steps.label: Hold the limit
steps.text:
He does not give her the sweets. He knows that if he does, she will learn that this works. He says, once, "No sweets today," and then stays where he is, quietly, his hand resting near her, ready if she reaches for him. He lets the storm run its course.

He also does not leave the queue. Abandoning the shop would end the scene and teach Ada that a tantrum gets her out of places she does not want to be.

He also says the limit once and then stops talking. Repeating it, explaining it or arguing about it would give her something to fight against, and keep the storm going.

steps.label: Comfort when it passes
steps.text:
After about two minutes, Ada's screams turn to sobs, and she crawls towards him. He picks her up and holds her against his chest, a hand on her back, breathing slowly. She shudders a few times and quietens. He says, "That was a big feeling," and pays for the shopping one-handed while she buries her face in his shoulder.

He also does not lecture her afterwards about behaving. A three-year-old who has just come through a storm needs comfort, not a lesson; the lesson is that the limit held.

He also lets her come to him rather than reaching for her. Her crawl towards him is her signal that she is ready to be held, and waiting for it makes the comfort hers to accept.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
In the car park, a woman who was behind them in the queue catches up and says that he handled it brilliantly, and that her own son did the same thing last week. Femi laughs and thanks her. He notes that the hardest part had been the first five seconds, when his own body wanted to end it at any cost, and that everything after that had followed from one slow breath and crouching down.

He also tells Ada's mother about it that evening, and they agree to keep sweets out of the conversation at checkouts for a while, which is easier than winning the same battle every week.

He also notes, for himself, that the tutting woman's disapproval had felt enormous in the moment and meant nothing an hour later, while how he treated Ada would stay with her.

moreFailures.title: Holding on when anger rises
moreFailures.body:
The most dangerous failure in this chapter is to keep holding a crying baby while frustration and anger build, out of a sense that you must not give up. Exhaustion and a baby who will not stop crying can push anyone towards a breaking point. The ICON messages are clear: infant crying is normal, comforting methods can help, it is okay to walk away, and never, ever shake a baby. If you feel anger or desperation rising, put the baby down safely on their back in their cot, leave the room, calm yourself for a few minutes, and go back. A crying baby in a safe cot is safe. If the feelings keep coming, tell your partner, your health visitor or your doctor.

It also helps to plan for the hardest times. Many parents find that the evening and the small hours are when crying is worst and patience thinnest. Knowing in advance what you will do, and who you will ring, makes it easier to do it.

It also helps to know that exhaustion is the biggest risk. Parents who are sleeping in short pieces for weeks are more likely to reach the edge, and sharing the night shifts, accepting help and sleeping when the baby sleeps are safety measures, not luxuries.

And remember that crying can sometimes be a sign that something is wrong. If a baby's cry sounds different from usual, or comes with a fever, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness or anything else that worries you, contact a health professional.

moreFailures.title: Parenting from above and behind a phone
moreFailures.body:
A father standing over a small child is a giant, and much of a child's experience of him comes through that height: a voice from above, a face a long way up, hands that reach down. A father whose face is turned to a phone is, to a baby, a still face that does not answer, which Tronick's studies showed distresses babies within seconds. Come down to the child's level when they are upset, when you set a limit and when you listen to something that matters to them, and give them a face that responds. Put the phone away for the moments that count.

It also helps to notice how much of a child's day is spent looking up at adults. Even a few minutes each day at their level, on the floor, playing their game, changes how they see you.

It also helps to notice your face when you listen to a child. A frown of concentration can look like disapproval to a small child, and a softer face tells them that what they are saying is welcome.

It also helps to answer babies' sounds and faces with your own. A baby who babbles and gets a babble back, or smiles and gets a smile back, is learning that the world responds to them.

moreFailures.title: Taking over the task
moreFailures.body:
When a child is slow or clumsy at something, it is tempting to take the tool and do it properly. The job gets done, and the child learns nothing except that their father does not trust them with it. Teaching from behind, with your hands over theirs, or from above, pointing, has the same effect. Sit beside them, at their height, with your hands near the job but not on it. Ask questions before giving answers. Demonstrate on a spare piece if you must, then give it back. Accept a wonky result that the child made over a perfect one that you did.

It also helps to notice when you take over for your own sake: because you are in a hurry, because you are embarrassed by a messy result, or because you enjoy the task. Naming your reason makes it easier to step back.

It also helps to remember that children learn more from struggle than from watching. A child who works out why the axle will not turn has learned something; a child who watches an adult fix it has learned only that adults can.

It also helps to notice your hands. If they keep drifting towards the task, put them in your lap or round a cup of tea. Keeping your hands busy elsewhere is one of the easiest ways to keep from taking over.

moreFailures.title: Rough play without brakes
moreFailures.body:
Physical play can be one of the best things a father offers, and it depends on the adult being in charge of it: keeping it safe, letting the child win sometimes, stopping when the child says stop, and calming things down before bed. Play that carries on after a child says stop, that frightens or hurts, or that the adult wins every time teaches the opposite of self-control. Young babies need their heads and necks supported and must never be shaken or thrown; rough-and-tumble is for older children, and only when it stays safe, fair and stoppable.

It also helps to wind down before bed. Rough play last thing at night often leads to children who cannot sleep. A calm game, a story or a bath does more for bedtime than another round of wrestling.

It also helps to give children a clear way to stop play themselves, such as a word or a tap, and to honour it every time. A child who knows the brake works is free to enjoy the speed.

It also helps to watch the other children, if there are several. Rough play between a father and one child can frighten a smaller sibling watching, and the youngest often needs a gentler game of their own.

questions.q: Can a father really comfort a newborn as well as a mother?
questions.a:
Many fathers can, with practice. Research suggests that fathers' bodies respond to parenthood too: Gettler and colleagues found that men who became fathers showed falls in testosterone, linked in the same group to more involvement in childcare. Erlandsson's small trial found that babies held skin to skin by their fathers after a caesarean birth calmed more quickly than babies in a cot. What makes a parent good at soothing is mostly time, practice and a calm body: a slow breath, a steady chest, a hand behind the head, a rhythm of walking or rocking. Fathers who hand the baby back every time never get the practice.

It also helps to share the hard times as well as the easy ones. Fathers who take some of the crying evenings, as well as the playful mornings, tend to become confident much sooner.

It also helps to find your own ways of soothing. Some fathers sing, some walk, some hum, some sway. Babies seem to care less about the method than about the steadiness of the person doing it.

And if you feel nervous holding a newborn, ask the midwife or health visitor to show you. Most fathers feel clumsy at first, and a few minutes of guidance can make an enormous difference to their confidence.

questions.q: What should I do if I feel angry with my crying baby?
questions.a:
Recognise that it is normal to feel it, and that what matters is what you do next. Put the baby down safely on their back in their cot, leave the room, and calm yourself for a few minutes: breathe slowly, splash cold water on your face, put on music, ring someone. Then go back and check on the baby. A crying baby in a safe cot is not in danger. Never shake a baby, even for a moment. If you feel this way often, or if the feelings frighten you, tell your partner, your health visitor or your doctor. Many parents feel it, and help is available.

It also helps to know that crying usually peaks in the first two or three months and then eases. Remembering that it will not last forever can make the worst nights easier to bear.

It also helps to know that walking away is not abandoning the baby. It is protecting both of you, and it is one of the most responsible things a tired parent can do.

questions.q: Is rough play good for children?
questions.a:
It seems to be, for older children, when it is done well. Amodia-Bidakowska, Laverty and Ramchandani's review of 78 studies found that fathers tended to play more physically than mothers and that father-child play was associated with children's later ability to manage their feelings and behaviour, though the findings were correlational. The key seems to be that the adult stays in charge: keeping the play safe, letting the child win sometimes, stopping when they say stop and winding down before bed. Babies should never be shaken or thrown, and their heads need support until they can hold them up themselves.

It also helps to watch the child's face for the moment the fun stops: wide eyes, a frown, laughter that becomes shrieking. Those are signs to slow down before the child has to say stop.

It also helps to let the child lead sometimes. A child who chooses when the wrestling starts and stops gets more from it than one who is always on the receiving end.

questions.q: How can I teach my child without taking over?
questions.a:
Use what Wood, Bruner and Ross called scaffolding: give just enough help for the child to do the next step themselves, and then step back. Sit beside them, at their height, with your hands near the task but not on it. Ask questions, such as "What do you think comes next?", before you give answers. If they are stuck, demonstrate on a spare piece rather than on theirs. Watch your own frustration, in your breath, jaw and hands, because children read it at once. Accept a result that is less neat than you would have made, because it is theirs.

It also helps to praise effort rather than results. "You kept trying with that axle" tells a child what mattered more than "Good job" does.

It also helps to resist the urge to correct every mistake. Some mistakes teach more if they are discovered later, and a child who finds their own error has learned something lasting.

It also helps to say out loud what you are doing when you step back: "I'm going to let you try this bit." Children often take the hint and rise to it.

questions.q: Is it wrong to tickle children?
questions.a:
Not if you stop when they say stop. Tickling can be great fun, and many children love it, but it produces laughter whether or not it is enjoyed, so a laughing child saying stop means stop. Stopping straight away, every time, teaches children that their no works, which matters for their safety as well as their trust in you. Some children, and some adults, do not like being tickled at all, and that is fine too. Ask, watch their body as well as their face, and let them start it again if they want to.

It also helps to teach children to stop as well. In play between siblings or friends, the same rule, stop means stop, protects everyone, and children who learn it at home tend to use it elsewhere.

It also helps to teach children to ask before tickling others, and to stop when others say stop. The rule protects them as well as their friends and siblings.

questions.q: How can I stay physically close to my son as he grows?
questions.a:
Keep offering, and let him choose. Many fathers stop hugging their sons somewhere around eight or ten, as if affection must end there, and many sons notice. Offer hugs, an arm round the shoulders or a hand on the back, especially at moments that matter: goodbyes, wins, losses, bad news. Accept a no gracefully. Make side-by-side time, as the opening chapter of this part described, because closeness often comes more easily beside him than face to face. As he gets older, the forms may change: a fist bump, a pull-in hug, a hand on the shoulder. The offer is what matters.

It also helps to tell him, as he grows, that the offer stands. "You're never too old for a hug from your dad" is a sentence many men wish they had heard.

It also helps to notice what he reaches for. Some boys stop wanting hugs but keep leaning against their fathers on the sofa, or asking for a lift so that they can talk in the car. Those are forms of closeness too.

It also helps to tell him, in words, that you are proud of him and glad to be his dad. Words of affection are a kind of touch too, and many men say they wish they had heard them more.

watch.title: The Pursuit of Happyness: Basketball and Dreams
watch.notice: A father on a basketball court with his young son. Watch his body move from play to something serious, and how he brings himself down to the boy's level to say it.

reviewPrompt: This week, come down to a child's eye level for every conversation that matters, and stop the moment a child says stop in play.
